prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: a locksmith who keeps one uncut key. Prose only, no headings.
text:
The shop smelled of ozone and old brass, a scent that clung to the back of Elias's throat like dust in sunlight. Behind his counter sat the display case where he sold new keys for cars with sleek digital fobs and apartment complexes guarded by keypad systems, but at the very center of the glass front lay it: a solitary key on its own velvet stand. It was an iron skeleton, filed down to a jagged point, bearing no brand name, no chip encoding, only the raw geometry of metal shaped against steel. The lockpick tools were arranged behind him in neat rows, each with a specific purpose for a specific tumblers mechanism, yet this one thing stood apart from all the rest.

Elias had possessed it since he was twenty-two and first learned that locks could be picked if you knew how to listen to their silence. He never cut duplicates of himself on his own front door; instead, he kept a master key for every lock in the city registry, but this specific piece remained uncut. It did not belong to any house or business he served. In fact, it was rumored by some clients that if you held up your car keys at night and found they matched nothing in his shop, you should come back later; Elias would let them keep their own locks intact while taking the original set as payment for a job well done, yet somehow managing to leave behind this phantom key.

The truth was far simpler than the rumor suggested. The uncut key opened no door that existed within four walls of his life. It belonged entirely to him, and its weight rested in his pocket like a heartbeat he could feel even when standing perfectly still at the counter. He carried it during rainstorms where water would soak through his jacket, dripping onto the floorboards with a rhythmic *plink-plunk* that matched the ticking of the wall clock inside. It did not fit any lock on earth; if forced into one, it simply jammed, useless and heavy as a stone. And yet, Elias refused to cut off its tip or file it down until he needed something else entirely, for fear of losing what made him feel whole in a world where everyone demanded copies of themselves.

People asked why he kept such an obsolete tool when the digital age had rendered physical keys nearly redundant except as fashion accessories. They said locks were becoming smart, requiring passwords and biometric scans rather than metal teeth to turn tumblers. But Elias knew better; every new encryption algorithm was just another way for humans to forget how things worked without their permission or consent. The uncut key represented something primal: the ability to start over if one chose to walk away from a life entirely, even though walking away meant leaving behind years of memories and faces known only through those same doors he could no longer open anymore.

He often sat at his kitchen table late into nights when business was slow, staring out the window toward rows of houses where lights flickered on and off in patterns that suggested sleep or wakefulness depending on who lived there inside them. Sometimes neighbors walked by carrying bags full of groceries while humming softly under their breaths; sometimes strangers drove past without looking twice at his signboard advertising locksmith services since dawn until dusk seven days a week straight away forevermore unless called out otherwise urgently during emergencies involving broken glass doors or stolen vehicles parked illegally overnight near trash cans overflowing with cardboard boxes left by lazy drivers who thought nobody cared enough to care about anything anymore anyway.

There were times when he felt the urge to discard it, perhaps melt it down and forge something new from its pure metal form so that someone else might find comfort in holding onto their own version of truth instead of pretending everything was fine despite all evidence suggesting otherwise right now today tomorrow next year forevermore until time runs out completely someday soon enough anyway. But then he remembered why he kept it: because sometimes people needed reminders that even if they lost their keys, there would always be someone willing to listen closely before trying anything else first thing in morning light breaking across empty streets filled with silence waiting patiently for footsteps approaching slowly from behind thick curtains hiding secrets long forgotten by those who once walked them daily without thinking twice about what lay beyond sightlines stretching endlessly far ahead straight toward horizon lines disappearing beneath clouds gathering overhead gently softly quietly peacefully forevermore.

The key was not merely an object; it was a promise made to himself years ago that he would never forget the feeling of holding onto something real in a world increasingly defined by illusions crafted from data points and algorithms designed to predict behavior based on past actions observed repeatedly over decades spanning generations alive today breathing air contaminated with smog particles rising up into sky above us all together now right here right now tonight tomorrow always.
topic: a locksmith who keeps one uncut key
